concepts: Study geological, soil, water and climate processes through field and laboratory evidence, geochemical and numerical models, ecological relationships and environmental responses. Energy systems and governance connect that scientific understanding to practical sustainability questions.

Investigate environmental change through GIS and remote sensing, programming, statistics, numerical methods and predictive models. Ground computational work in Earth-system, climate, soil and water mechanisms, while examining adaptation and governance.

Study how soil and water processes interact with biodiversity, ecosystems and land use. Combine geoscience and environmental chemistry with ecological measurement, conservation, farming, nature-based water management and environmental justice.
conceptFreeze.decision: Preserve the strongest Earth-system concept and sequentially retain two distinct responses supported by climate/geospatial and soil/water/biosphere interests. Clarify the computational programme label; numerical/AI methods support environmental evidence and do not constitute dedicated atmospheric physics. Changes follow these concepts, not a course-difference quota.

courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.rationale: Required Year1 personal and academic development.

availableEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
availableEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
availableEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courses.rationale: Chemical/thermodynamic/mechanical principles, nutrient and carbon boundaries, elementary differential models and laboratory measurement provide direct foundations for Earth-system processes. Its biopolymer experiment is a material-science practical, not hydrological field measurement.

availableEvidence.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
availableEvidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.

availableEvidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

courses.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
courses.rationale: Organismal/phylogenetic diversity, ecological roles, biodiversity indices, identification and data collection/analysis give concrete biosphere knowledge and measurement for Earth-system and ecosystem questions.

availableEvidence.description2: The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and health.
availableEvidence.profile: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.

availableEvidence.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis

courses.name: Introduction to Programming
courses.rationale: Python control flow, collections, functions, recursion, object-oriented construction and testing/debugging supply concrete scientific-computing foundations. Environmental datasets are possible applications, not guaranteed gateway content.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.

courses.rationale: Actual wave physics, optical spectroscopy, chemical analysis, microscopic materials and stress/strain supply physical and chemical methods for geoscience and environmental evidence. The final greenwashing communication project is not integrated Earth-system modelling.

availableEvidence.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
availableEvidence.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.rationale: Calculus, optimisation, differential equations, dynamic-model implementation and numerical approximation supply actual quantitative tools for environmental process models. The selected detailed evidence is not a separate linear-algebra sequence.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.

courses.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations
courses.rationale: The available description substantively supports geoscience risk analysis, climate-related/mining disasters, drought and toxic-algal hazards and adaptation. It supplies direct environmental-risk content without invented modelling software or field assessment methods.

availableEvidence.description2: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.

courses.name: Earth System Science Tools
courses.rationale: The description directly supports biosphere/hydrosphere/lithosphere/atmosphere interactions, system modelling, proxies/isotope tracers and past/future climate, with a greenhouse-gas-pathways field trip. These receive full consideration; particular tracer protocols or software are not inferred.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

courses.name: Climate Change
courses.rationale: Greenhouse gases, feedbacks/tipping points, sea-level/ocean/ecological impacts and mitigation/adaptation provide substantive climate-system knowledge. Stakeholder interviews and a climate film do not constitute quantitative atmospheric-dynamics training.

availableEvidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.

courses.name: Dynamic Earth
courses.rationale: Rocks/minerals, sedimentation/facies, structural deformation, stratigraphy and tectonic/geophysical processes directly implement geological Earth science, including field mapping, cross-sections and reconstruction of geological history.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. availableEvidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. courses.name: Earth's Resources
courses.rationale: The description supports substantial geoscientific research on nuclear-waste storage, geothermal energy and CO2 capture through literature review, reports and professional presentation. This is direct subsurface/resource inquiry, not documented lowland sedimentary logging or a required bachelor thesis.

availableEvidence.description2: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability
courses.rationale: Food/water/energy/climate governance, institutions, power, stakeholders and policy-option appraisal provide specific tools for assessing responses to environmental change. The Zeeland policy project does not substitute for hydrological or geological science.

availableEvidence.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
availableEvidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.

upstreamAmbiguityCheck.resolution: Selected detailed evidence concerns calculus/differential equations/dynamic models. Do not claim a separate linear-algebra sequence from the shorter official description; a separate LinearAlgebra course is selected in the computational option.

findings: The closest response materially addresses defining Earth-science substance through actual geology/field reconstruction, soil/aquifer field/lab/geophysics, environmental geochemistry/speciation, Earth-system proxies/tracers/modelling, GIS, climate mechanisms and water/delta processes. Mathematics, statistics, computation, ecosystems and energy responses support this core. General sustainability coherence alone is not the justification.

The second concept changes the academic priority toward spatial observation and quantitative/predictive evidence. Linear algebra, algorithms, image processing and neural models are substantive methods and join actual Earth Observation/soil/climate courses. Its old atmosphere-heavy label overstated dedicated physics; the revised label describes its actual content and does not promise a satellite/forecasting project.

The third concept substantively combines soil/water mechanisms with ecological conditions, biodiversity/evolution, conservation, marine/coastal processes, farming/land-use effects, nature-based adaptation and environmental justice. Molecular/cellular/metabolic/genetic content is a specific biological foundation, placed before advanced ecological inquiry; human disease is not its organising subject.

All35course contributions were read against actual descriptions/profiles/topics/methods. Description-only NaturalHazards, EarthSystemScienceTools, EarthsResources, RenewableSystemDesign and EnvironmentalJustice receive full consideration within their stated subject/method scope. No enrichment was fabricated and no selected course was excluded merely for lacking an outline.

Six original offering violations are repaired. DynamicEarth moves to Fall2027 in all three plans. ResearchInASustainableDelta has only a Fall2026 offering and is removed rather than restored or inserted before the desired foundations. Climate-response energy study replaces it in closest/ecological plans; probability adds actual uncertainty methods in the computational plan. The computational plan replaces energy-design emphasis with neural data methods; the ecology plan replaces energy-design with farming/land-use appraisal. These follow the frozen concepts, not arbitrary distinctness swaps.

Every plan has24unique7.5ECcourses,6terms of4,Year1PPD and6advanced courses, with earlier formal prerequisites and currentXofferings. All pairwise differences are substantive and37.5/52.5/75EC each way. Advisory preparation is considered; open-curriculum rules permit EarthSystemTools after SustainabilityEssentialsI before DynamicEarth, since no geology prerequisite exists.

Reassessed all31external placements:15specific partial correspondences and16meaningful gaps. Calculus aligns directly with MathematicalMethods; ecological theory aligns with EcosystemsUncovered rather than coupled evapotranspiration/transport. EarthsResources is not documented lowland sedimentology; no taught research course is aligned to the individual thesis. Data-skills correspondence identifies actual data handling, not generic research function. Every positive rationale records limits in scope.

Atmospheric forcing/climate feedbacks are an important shared part of IntroductionAtmosphere; dedicated thermodynamics/cloud/dynamics/air-quality depth remains explicit. Aquifer characterization, soil remediation and catchment-water issues likewise support bounded correspondence without implying full flow-modelling, soil-quality or field-course equivalence.
